title: CRP Levels: What's Normal, High & Dangerous (Chart)
summary: See the reference categories for standard CRP and hs-CRP, what can raise CRP, and how to respond to an elevated result.
body_markdown:
Table of contents


C-reactive protein (CRP) is a blood marker that typically rises when inflammation is active in your body. This guide shows the reference categories for standard CRP and hs-CRP, the common causes of an elevated result, and how to tell a temporary spike from a number worth acting on.


A high result shows that inflammation may be present, but not its cause or location. Whether a number matters depends on which assay was used, your symptoms, and your health history, so start with the chart and then place your result in context.


## TL;DR


- Standard CRP and high-sensitivity CRP measure the same protein at different concentration ranges.
- Standard CRP is commonly used when evaluating or monitoring larger inflammatory responses.
- hs-CRP measures lower concentrations and may add information to an overall cardiovascular-risk assessment.
- Neither assay diagnoses the cause of inflammation or determines urgency from a number alone.
- Use the reporting laboratory’s reference information. If a result is unexpected, persistent, or accompanied by symptoms, review it with your doctor.


## CRP levels chart


Read your result against the units and reference interval printed on your own report; laboratories differ. These categories are the broad map most reports fit into.


Standard CRP is often reported in mg/L or mg/dL, and 1 mg/dL equals 10 mg/L:


Standard CRP result Common description


Within the laboratory’s reference interval No elevation detected relative to that interval


Above the interval, below 10 mg/L (1 mg/dL) A smaller inflammatory response may be present


10 to 100 mg/L (1 to 10 mg/dL) Often described as a moderate increase


Above 100 mg/L (above 10 mg/dL) Often described as a marked increase


hs-CRP is reported in mg/L and read in a cardiovascular context. These historical bands provide context, not a risk score:


hs-CRP result Historical cardiovascular-risk band


Below 1 mg/L Lower


1 to 3 mg/L Intermediate


Above 3 mg/L Higher


Two thresholds from current guidance sit alongside those bands:


- 2 mg/L or higher on more than one occasion is treated as a risk-enhancing factor in current prevention guidance.
- Above 10 mg/L often reflects an acute inflammatory response rather than your usual baseline. Retest when you are well.


No single CRP number is “dangerous” for every person. Urgency depends on symptoms and the underlying cause, and the sections below explain how to place your result in context.


## Inflammation 101: acute and chronic inflammation


Inflammation is part of the body’s response to infection, injury, and other health conditions. It can be short-lived, as during healing, or persist when an inflammatory condition or exposure continues.


Long-term inflammation is associated with several chronic conditions, but an association does not mean that a CRP result proves a condition is present or caused it. CRP is one piece of clinical information, not a direct measurement of every inflammatory process in the body.


Acute and chronic inflammation can overlap. An infection may temporarily raise CRP in someone who also has a long-term inflammatory condition, while some inflammatory conditions may not produce a large CRP increase at all. This is why symptoms, timing, and the reason for testing matter as much as the number.


## What does a CRP blood test measure?


The liver makes C-reactive protein in response to inflammation. CRP levels can rise and fall as inflammatory activity changes.


A CRP result is nonspecific. It may help show whether inflammation is present or changing, but it does not show where the inflammation is located. Diagnosis requires the result to be considered with symptoms, medical history, examination, and other testing.


## Standard CRP versus high-sensitivity CRP


Both tests look for the same protein; they differ in how low they can measure and the question they are used to answer.


Test What the assay is designed to measure Common clinical context


Standard CRP Larger changes in CRP concentration Evaluating or monitoring infection, injury, inflammatory conditions, or response to treatment


High-sensitivity CRP Lower CRP concentrations with greater precision Adding information to an overall cardiovascular-risk assessment


An hs-CRP test does not replace cholesterol, blood pressure, smoking history, diabetes status, or other established cardiovascular-risk information. See[CRP versus hs-CRP](https://mitohealth.com/compare/crp-vs-hscrp) for a focused comparison.


## How to read CRP levels in context


Units deserve special care: 1 mg/dL equals 10 mg/L, so confusing them creates a tenfold interpretation error. Check which unit your report uses before comparing it with any chart, including the one above. Reference intervals also differ between laboratories, so the interval printed on your report takes precedence over a threshold copied from anywhere else.


Standard CRP result pattern What it may tell you What it cannot tell you by itself


Within the laboratory’s reference interval The assay did not detect an elevation relative to that reference interval That no inflammation or health condition is present


Mildly above the reference interval A smaller inflammatory response may be present Whether the cause is temporary, chronic, or clinically important


Markedly above the reference interval A larger inflammatory response may be present and deserves clinical context A specific diagnosis, cause, location, or treatment


A change from a prior result Inflammatory activity may have changed Why it changed or whether the tests are comparable


The moderate and marked categories in the chart above come from MedlinePlus. They describe the size of the inflammatory response, not its urgency; symptoms and the underlying cause determine that.


### Does a normal CRP rule out inflammation?


No. A result within the laboratory’s reference interval means this assay did not detect an elevation relative to that interval. It does not rule out every infection, autoimmune condition, localized inflammatory process, or other health problem.


Standard CRP may also be the wrong assay when the clinical question concerns lower CRP concentrations and cardiovascular risk. That is where hs-CRP may be considered, but hs-CRP is not a general test for every form of hidden inflammation.


## How to interpret hs-CRP for cardiovascular risk


hs-CRP belongs within an overall cardiovascular-risk assessment, not in the standard-CRP categories above. The chart’s historical bands (below 1, 1 to 3, and above 3 mg/L) and its 2 mg/L risk-enhancing threshold come from different guidelines and answer different questions, which is why a single threshold should not be read without knowing the guideline behind it. None of them diagnose cardiovascular disease or determine treatment on their own, and none apply during an acute illness.


Evidence about how much hs-CRP improves traditional risk prediction has not always been consistent. Because CRP can vary within the same person, recent inflammation may also affect whether a result reflects your usual baseline. If hs-CRP is above 10 mg/L, retest when you are well so an acute inflammatory response is not mistaken for your usual baseline.


For definitions, units, and interpretation limitations, see the[hs-CRP biomarker reference](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/hscrp) .


## What can cause an elevated CRP result?


An elevated CRP result can occur in more than one context. Examples include:


- **Infection or acute illness:** bacterial and viral infections can raise CRP, sometimes substantially.
- **Injury, surgery, or tissue inflammation:** CRP may rise while the body responds and heals.
- **Autoimmune or inflammatory conditions:** rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, vasculitis, inflammatory bowel disease, and other conditions may affect CRP, although the marker behaves differently across diseases and people.
- **Long-term metabolic and cardiovascular context:** obesity and some chronic conditions are associated with higher CRP, but CRP alone cannot diagnose them.
- **Smoking and environmental exposures:** tobacco smoke and some pollutants can contribute to chronic inflammatory signaling.
- **Hormonal and personal factors:** pregnancy, estrogen-containing medicines, sleep problems, age, and sex may influence a result or its interpretation.


This list is not diagnostic. A CRP value cannot distinguish among these possibilities, and a normal result does not rule out every inflammatory condition.


## Can lifestyle changes lower CRP?


Lifestyle changes can lower CRP for some people when the elevated result reflects modifiable inflammation, cardiometabolic risk, smoking, sleep disruption, or excess visceral fat. They are not a substitute for diagnosing infection, autoimmune disease, injury, or another medical cause.


The right response depends on why CRP is elevated. Evidence supports discussing these foundations as part of overall health rather than treating them as a guaranteed way to reach a specific CRP number:


- **Avoid smoking:** smoking contributes to cardiovascular risk and systemic inflammation.
- **Move regularly:** aerobic and resistance exercise can support cardiovascular and metabolic health. Very intense exercise can temporarily affect inflammatory markers, so test timing matters.
- **Choose a sustainable dietary pattern:** patterns emphasizing vegetables, fruit, legumes, whole grains, nuts, fish, and unsaturated fats can support cardiovascular health.
- **Protect sleep:** poor sleep and sleep disorders can affect inflammatory and cardiometabolic health.
- **Review weight and metabolic health without reducing the issue to weight alone:** changes in visceral fat, glucose regulation, and other risk factors may matter alongside CRP.
- **Address the underlying condition:** infection, autoimmune disease, injury, or another medical cause requires condition-specific evaluation rather than generic “CRP lowering.”


Do not start a supplement, follow an extreme diet, or pursue a specific reduction target solely because of one result. For a detailed review of interventions and monitoring, see[how to lower CRP and inflammation](https://mitohealth.com/guide/lowering-crp-inflammation-naturally) .


## What about medicines?


Medicines can change CRP when they treat the condition driving inflammation, but CRP is not the treatment target in every situation. Treatment choices depend on the diagnosis, symptoms, and overall risk.


Some treatments used for cardiovascular, autoimmune, infectious, or other conditions may lower or raise CRP as inflammation changes. Do not start, stop, or change a prescription because of a CRP result without speaking with your doctor or prescribing clinician.


## What should you do after an elevated result?


After an elevated CRP result, first identify whether the test was standard CRP or hs-CRP and whether a temporary trigger could explain it. Then decide whether symptoms, medical history, or repeat testing make the result actionable.


Start with the clinical context rather than trying to lower the laboratory number on its own:


1. Confirm whether the report is standard CRP or hs-CRP.
2. Check the units and the reporting laboratory’s reference information.
3. Consider whether illness, injury, surgery, or another temporary source of inflammation was present around the test.
4. Consider symptoms, medical history, medicines, supplements, and other test results together. If the result is unexplained or you have symptoms, review it with your doctor.
5. Decide whether repeat testing could provide a more representative result and when it should occur.


Do not start, stop, or change a prescription medicine or supplement solely because of a CRP result. Treatment depends on the underlying clinical question, not just the marker.


For a detailed look at lifestyle changes and retesting timelines, continue to[how to lower CRP and inflammation](https://mitohealth.com/guide/lowering-crp-inflammation-naturally) .


## Questions to ask about your result


The most useful CRP follow-up questions clarify the assay, the units, the likely trigger, and the decision the result is meant to support.


- Was this standard CRP or high-sensitivity CRP?
- Are the units mg/L or mg/dL?
- Does the result fit the laboratory’s reference information?
- Could a recent illness, injury, procedure, medicine, or hard workout have affected it?
- Is repeat testing useful, and if so, when?
- Which symptoms, diagnoses, or cardiovascular risk factors matter most in my case?
- What outcome are we trying to monitor rather than simply lowering the number?


## When the individual hs-CRP test is relevant


The individual hs-CRP test is relevant when the question is specifically about low-level CRP measurement, often in a cardiovascular-risk context. Standard CRP and hs-CRP measure the same protein, but hs-CRP is designed for lower concentrations.


If your question is specifically about the high-sensitivity measurement, view the[individual hs-CRP test](https://mitohealth.com/products/c-reactive-protein-high-sensitivity-hs-crp) . Current pricing and availability are on the product page.


For help choosing between the individual test and a broader panel that includes hs-CRP, see the[hs-CRP blood test guide](https://mitohealth.com/blog/a-guide-on-hs-crp-test-for-inflammation-and-heart-health) .
